I wonder whether the minister might resolve a few problems that I have. I understand that the tuition fees for unemployed Hungarian refugees wishing to attend night school are paid by the department and yet the same fees are not paid for unemployed immigrants from other countries. I refer in particular to immigrants out of Holland who are unemployed on the west coast and who are attending night school. They find that they cannot obtain free tuition; yet Hungarian refugees who are unemployed are able to do so. There is quite a bit of resentment at the discrimination. It may be that the British Columbia department of education is at fault. I wish the minister would clarify the matter and say exactly who it is that is paying the fees of the unemployed Hungarian refugees

fees for the unemployed immigrants from other parts of the world.
The other question I had is this. For how long is a sponsor responsible for the welfare of an immigrant into Canada? Is it now for a one-year period, a two-year period or a five-year period? I have had some reports that the regulation with regard to this matter has been altered of late. I should appreciate being informed as to what the situation is now. Has the minister ever considered that the federal government ought to assume responsibilities for the health and welfare of immigrants until the expiration of the five-year period? I understand that at the present time the federal government assumes responsibility only for a very limited time for the welfare in Canada of immigrants and that thereafter it becomes the responsibility of the provincial and municipal governments. I feel that here again is one more instance where the federal government might relieve the municipal treasuries of a burden.
I think the federal government ought to assume responsibility for a 5-year period at least. That is accepted as the period during which men must remain here before they can become Canadian citizens, and I think they should be regarded as wards, if you like, or at least as the responsibility of the federal machine.
I wish the minister could also give us a statement as to the refugee position in western Europe. How many displaced persons are still in camps, hospitals and sanatoria there? Has the government accepted any of these people recently, and is it entertaining taking in some of these refugees who for reasons of health are not able to comply with the regulations? I think, Mr. Chairman, that Canadians would be much happier if we accepted our share of the sick people and looked after them in our own country rather than help some international organization to look after them in these refugee camps.
I think the same feeling exists in Canada with regard to the refugees in the Middle East. I see our government is spending $1 million this year for the relief or welfare of refugees in the Middle East. Some rapid calculation would show that if we spent the same amount of money in looking after them in our own country not only would it help to solve the refugee problem but it would help the economy of our nation. After all, I would prefer to have them here and feed them on Canadian wheat than to pay Canadian money to buy United States wheat with which to feed them.
I wish to express to the minister my appreciation of the efforts the officers of his department have made in all the immigration

cases I have called to their attention during the past five years. I can say that not one worthy case has been refused admission to Canada. That is my experience, and I am very grateful for the assistance that has been given. The officers have gone to great lengths to find out what the difficulty was in every case. That may not be the experience of all hon. members but it has been my experience.
And now I wonder whether the minister could say whether or not there is any "follow up" in the case of sponsored immigrants. If a Canadian sponsors an immigrant and the department hears no complaint, and no one brings the immigrant to the attention of the department, does the department completely forget the immigrant once he has passed the immigration officers at the point of landing? I have in mind a number of cases where sponsors have illegally brought immigrants to Canada by agreeing to supply employment, knowing well that they have no such intention. Then, when the immigrant arrives, he is fobbed off on some restaurant proprietor who works him for 70 hours a week at 50 cents an hour, year in and year out. These people have no chance, working these long hours, of learning the language. They do not know what their rights are; they do not know how they are protected by the labour laws as to holidays with pay, and so on, and these laws are constantly violated. I think that a visit once a year by immigration officers to such immigrants to find out what they are doing, what wages they are receiving and under what conditions they have to work would serve a very useful purpose. Not only would it help the immigrant but it would remove much of the hard feeling that exists at present because many Canadian workers feel immigrants are competing unfairly by accepting positions at substandard rates of pay and working hours.

With regard to the question of responsibility for sponsored immigrants, the answer is that whereas in former years there was an actual undertaking in the sponsorship form covering a period of years, the principle now is that the sponsor is responsible for the immigrant only until he is established, and that, of course, must be a flexible period.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext: What does that mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext:
Until he is placed in employment-until he is established in a job at a proper standard of wages on the basis of which he is able to support himself in this country. I think the hon. member would agree it would be undesirable to insist that immigrants should remain in a particular location. There must be a stage at which immigrants are on their own and able to move around the country. It would be unrealistic as well as terribly expensive to attempt to hold the sponsor rigidly to the responsibility of an individual who after being successfully placed in employment in Ottawa leaves of his own volition to go to Winnipeg or Vancouver and becomes unemployed there. It is our feeling that the sponsor has discharged his responsibility when he has seen to it that the immigrant is placed in the employment which he has undertaken to find for him.
With regard to the last part of my hon. friend's remarks in respect of immigrants being exploited by unscrupulous operators, I am informed that of last year's immigrant move of 282,164, about 120,000 fell into the category of sponsored immigrants. I am sure, therefore, that the hon. member will appreciate it would be physically and financially impossible for the department to maintain or to keep physical contact with each of these men. We do our best but we do admit that we do not know all the details of every case and I must ask, therefore, that if the hon. gentleman has knowledge of a case such as this he should bring it to our attention privately or publicly as he prefers and we would be glad to follow it up.

I have some doubts as to whether we have any right to send inspectors into the kitchens of establishments in the manner suggested by the hon. member. Minimum wages are a matter of provincial

Supply-Citizenship and Immigration responsibility. What we can do is help when a case is brought to our attention of an immigrant who is being exploited, but without answering further I think we would be open to very proper criticism if federal immigration inspectors entered commercial establishments and demanded answers to certain questions. I would hope that the information would come the other way, that those interested in such cases would persuade the immigrants who are exploited to bring their cases to our attention. We could then take up the case with the provincial minimum wage officers and set in motion the necessary machinery to see that these immigrants are protected and not exploited.
With regard to the question as to the length of time for which the dominion government is responsible for immigrants after their arrival in Canada, the normal period is 12 months, on the basis that it is desirable that an immigrant should become integrated as soon as possible into the municipal, provincial and other local aspects of society in which he lives and should no longer be in a position different from that of the ordinary Canadian citizen or even a landed immigrant, and that position is one of looking to the federal government and the responsibility of it; but while that is the period in which we normally assume responsibility there is no hard and fast line drawn. Cases have to be looked at on their individual merits. We certainly wish to be held not responsible after 12 months, but in a winter such as this, with a very heavy immigration intake, as there has been, we realize that we cannot be dogmatic about the matter. There are discussions under way with the provinces now as to certain arrangements in view of the unusual circumstances that obtain this winter.
The state of the refugees in western Europe is not a matter on which we have statistics of our own. The general survey is maintained by the United Nations and the figures can be obtained. If the hon. gentleman wishes it, one of the officials will obtain the figures and provide them to him later.
With regard to the program for the emptying of the camps, I am glad to be able to say we have recently had discussions with Dr. Lindt, the United Nations high commissioner for refugees, who outlined the problem to us and indicated that he would be bringing to the attention of interested governments a survey of the facts and would discuss with us later proposals for taking care of that situation. I must say with regard to the hon. member's proposal, that if we were to bring

these men over here in large numbers and undertake to provide them with medical and other treatment and care in Canada this action would be the cause of a great deal of concern on the part of the provinces whose responsibility it is to provide for hospital and other kinds of medical attention. It is not a matter we could enter into lightly, because the burden would immediately fall on the provinces, but we are expecting to have further consultations with the United Nations high commissioner for refugees on the general refugee situation in western Europe.

speechtext: I believe this is the right item on which to ask the minister about the situation at Hong Kong. I understand there is a very heavy list of prospective immigrants who have applied. I have been advised of one case where the would-be immigrant was told to come back in approximately nine months' time. The list of applicants is so heavy and the number of officers is so limited that some Canadians are beginning to think it is a deliberate policy of the government to have only a limited number of officers there in order to slow down the flow of immigration through Hong Kong. As the minister knows, the situation over there is rather serious in that the city is plugged with some million and a half refugees. Some of these refugees are relatives of Canadian citizens. Some of our most reputable citizens have relatives among these refugees. What is the department doing to relieve the present situation?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext: The situation in Hong Kong is a baffling one and not one which I believe can be solved simply by an increase in staff. There are questions of identification, difficulties in getting information in regard to the background of these people, tracing their family relationships, medical examinations and so on. All these things are matters where the success of the operation is really dependent, I think, not so much upon the number of staff as upon the skill and knowledge of the staff regarding the conditions of the people with whom they are dealing. Last fall we sent an extra officer over there. We have increased the staff by one officer who can speak both English and Chinese. He is highly trained in Chinese. While I know the situation is not satisfactory, I can report to the hon. gentleman that in the month of December, 1957, we admitted from Hong Kong 206 Chinese compared with 77 in the month of December, 1956.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN

strictly limiting factors with regard to our ability to deal with the number of applications we have from Italy.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext: What is the situation at the present time with regard to India? speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext: No, there is no increase in the field staff in India. The quota for India was set less than a year ago. It was set in May, 1957, when it was increased to 300. While I have had under consideration the question of some further negotiations, these are matters which you do not open too frequently as between governments. Furthermore, we had hoped to be able to deal with a considerable portion of the backlog as a result of the order in council of January 2, and until we see what effect that has in relieving pressure on the quota numbers we will not really be able to make an intelligent assessment of just what further quota number we should ask for.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext: How do you decide what the quota is to be?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: IMMIGRATION TO CANADA BY ETHNIC ORIGIN
speechtext:
As a matter of fact, of course, it will depend in part on what the views of the other government are and also upon the pressure that is exerted in this country for the admission of people from the country from which they are being applied for.
Before I make any further decision I want to see whether, in fact, the amendment that was brought into force on January 2 will relieve the pressure and enable us to take care of the volume of applications we are receiving. If I find it does not, then I shall be prepared to have a further look at the situation.

Ottawa, December 21, 1957. My dear Premier:
I have your telegram of December 21 in regard to the application of thermo-power agreements to the province of Newfoundland.
I am asking my colleague, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, to look into this matter and get in touch with you. I know that he will be glad to see what can be done to bring Newfoundland clearly within the terms of the proposed agreements.
May I express my best wishes for the holiday season,
I am,

The Honourable J. R. Smallwood, M.L.A., Premier of Newfoundland,
Legislative Building,
St. John's, Newfoundland.
Ottawa 4, Canada, January 8, 1958.
The Honourable J. R. Smallwood,
Premier of Newfoundland,
St. John's, Newfoundland.
My dear Premier,
I refer to your telegram and the reply from the Prime Minister, both dated December 21, concerning the application to Newfoundland of the legislation now before parliament with regard to thermal power in the Atlantic provinces. The Prime Minister asked me to get in touch with you further about the points you raised.
For your information I am enclosing herewith a copy of the bill that has now received
first reading in the House of Commons. As you will note, it is drafted in terms sufficiently wide that agreements can be made, within its provisions, with any of the Atlantic provinces. In short, the kind of arrangement that is being made with New Brunswick and with Nova Scotia, or a modification of it, could be made with the province of Newfoundland if the government of Newfoundland so desired.
You suggest in your telegram that "the word thermal would in practice virtually eliminate Newfoundland from any assistance from Ottawa". I think this impression arises from a misunderstanding. As you will note from an examination of the bill, it is only thermal power plants that come under its terms. Hydroelectric power plants are not covered by this legislation. However, the interconnection and transmission fines and related facilities that can be built are not limited to fines for the transmission of power produced in thermal electric plants. It would thus be quite possible to enter into an agreement with the government of Newfoundland for the provision of transmission and interconnection fines which, as you know, are often very costly and of great importance in the development of any power system.
In the case of hydroelectric plants there has, as you know, been an arrangement made with New Brunswick for the financing on an eight-year basis of the Beechwood plant. The Prime Minister has indicated that a similar arrangement could be made in other instances if an equally valid case for such financial assistance could be shown. The speech from the throne on October 14 also indicated that the government is prepared to enter into a joint program with British Columbia to develop the power of the Columbia river. I have been authorized by the government to say that if major hydroelectric projects elsewhere in Canada were to lend themselves to the possibility of a joint program on the same sort of basis the government would be prepared to give consideration to such a proposal. Conceivably this is the sort of thing that might be of interest to Newfoundland.
From what I have said you will appreciate that the policies that have been announced by the government with respect to power developments have had particular regard for the special problems of the Atlantic area and have also differentiated as between thermal and hydroelectric projects. It is, however, quite apparent that the programs do not by any means exclude Newfoundland from benefit under them.
Yours sincerely,
Alvin Hamilton.
